title: Disney Cuts Hundreds of Jobs With Pixar Bearing the Brunt
excerpt: Pixar Animation Studios faces the deepest cuts in Disney's third round of layoffs under CEO Josh D'Amaro, even as the studio rides a $1.2 billion box office year.
body:
• Disney is laying off several hundred employees on Tuesday, with Pixar Animation Studios absorbing the largest share of cuts among the company's film divisions.
  • The layoffs also hit ESPN, Disney Entertainment Television, and National Geographic, marking the third major round of job eliminations under CEO Josh D'Amaro's "One Disney" restructuring.
  • Pixar is adopting a "long and lean" production model that caps future films at 16,500 person-weeks of labor, down from as many as 20,000 on prior productions.
  • The cuts come during a strong commercial year for Pixar, whose releases have already grossed more than $1.2 billion at the global box office in 2026.

The Walt Disney Company began notifying hundreds of employees on Tuesday that their positions have been eliminated, with Pixar Animation Studios taking the heaviest hit among the entertainment giant's film operations. The layoffs span multiple divisions, including ESPN, Disney Entertainment Television, and National Geographic, according to The Hollywood Reporter.

According to The Wrap, roughly 150 Pixar staffers were impacted — slightly fewer than the 175 positions eliminated during the studio's record 2024 layoffs. Employees were informed Tuesday morning.

A 'Long and Lean' Shift at Pixar

The reductions at Pixar are tied to a fundamental restructuring of how the studio makes films. Sources at the company told Cartoon Brew that Pixar earlier this year announced it would adopt a "long and lean" production schedule. Under the new model, future films will be capped at 16,500 person-weeks of labor — a sharp reduction from the 18,500 to 20,000 person-weeks typical of previous productions.

The shift amounts to a roughly 15 to 18 percent cut in the total labor budget per film, requiring smaller teams to work over longer timelines. For a studio that has long prided itself on iterative, labor-intensive filmmaking, the change represents a significant recalibration.

"Given the fast-moving pace of our industries, this requires us to constantly assess how to foster a more agile and technologically-enabled workforce to meet tomorrow's needs."

— Josh D'Amaro, CEO, The Walt Disney Company

Third Round of Cuts Under D'Amaro

Tuesday's layoffs are the third major reduction since Josh D'Amaro succeeded Bob Iger as Disney's CEO. The company unified its marketing departments under Chief Marketing Officer Asad Ayaz in January, resulting in initial job losses. A broader wave followed in April, when Disney eliminated approximately 1,000 positions across the company, including about 8 percent of Marvel's workforce.

This latest round, while smaller than the April cuts, extends the restructuring to key creative and operational units. At ESPN, the layoffs are partly driven by the network's absorption of NFL Network earlier this year. ESPN chairman Jimmy Pitaro said in a memo to employees that the company had been "carefully evaluating our collective teams, resources and organizational structure" following the NFL acquisition. On-air talent affected includes SportsCenter anchor Karl Ravech and NFL analyst Ryan Clark.

National Geographic is the hardest-hit segment under Disney Entertainment Television, though specific numbers for that division have not been disclosed.

Strong Box Office, Smaller Teams

The timing of the Pixar cuts stands out. The studio has had its best commercial year in recent memory. Toy Story 5 has earned $958 million globally and is still in theaters, while original film Hoppers grossed $223.5 million. Together with other releases, Pixar has crossed $1.2 billion at the worldwide box office in 2026 — a performance that underscores the tension between financial results and corporate belt-tightening.

However, some reports suggest Hoppers, while profitable, underperformed Disney's internal expectations, contributing to the calculus behind the reductions. The broader "long and lean" strategy signals that Disney intends to make Pixar sustainably profitable at lower cost, even during strong years.

What It Means for the Animation Workforce

For Indian-origin professionals in Hollywood's animation and VFX pipeline, the layoffs add to an already uncertain landscape. Indian talent has a significant presence in U.S. animation studios, particularly in technical and artistic roles at companies like Pixar, DreamWorks, and Illumination. Successive rounds of cuts at major studios — Disney, Paramount Skydance, and Sony Pictures have all announced layoffs in recent months — tighten the available positions in an industry that many Indian professionals entered on H-1B and O-1 visas.

The visa dependency makes studio layoffs particularly consequential: workers on employer-sponsored visas face a 60-day grace period to find new employment or risk losing their immigration status.

What's Next

Disney has not indicated whether further layoffs are planned, but D'Amaro's emphasis on an "agile" and "technologically-enabled workforce" suggests the restructuring is far from over. The company employed approximately 231,000 people as of September 2025. With D23, Disney's marquee fan event, approaching later this month, the company will likely pivot attention toward its creative pipeline even as the organizational reshaping continues behind the scenes.
